Alright, I've just finished laying down the core pieces of the Glint CLI: configuration constants, a logger, diagnostics handling, and the Groq API wrapper. The next logical piece is the protocol layer that will let the model communicate tool calls back to the CLI, since Groq's compound model doesn't support native function calling. I need a deterministic, collision‑free way for the model to embed tool invocation data in its text output, and a set of utilities to parse, strip, and format those calls.

First, I should define clear sentinel strings that are unlikely to appear in normal output or in Groq’s internal <tool> tags. Something like `<<<glint:tool` to open a block and `>>>glint` to close it seems safe and readable. These will be exported as constants so other modules (e.g., the UI renderer and the Groq wrapper) can reference them.

Next, I need a TypeScript interface for a parsed tool call: it should capture the tool name, its arguments (as a generic record), and the raw block text for debugging. I'll call this `ToolCall`.

Parsing will involve a regular expression that matches any number of lines between the open and close sentinels, allowing optional whitespace before each sentinel. The regex should be global and multiline so I can iterate with `matchAll`. I'll store it as `BLOCK_RE`.

The `parseToolCalls` function will iterate over all matches, trim the captured body, and then attempt to parse it as JSON. Since the model might wrap the JSON in markdown fences or include stray whitespace, I need a lenient parser. I'll write a helper `parseJsonLenient` that strips leading/trailing backticks and attempts JSON.parse; if that fails, it will locate the first `{` and manually walk the string, tracking braces while respecting string literals and escapes, to extract a balanced JSON object. This mirrors the approach I've used before for robust parsing.

After extracting a valid JSON object, I should verify it has a `tool` string property before constructing a `ToolCall` entry. The raw block is also kept for possible logging.

I also need a utility to strip all tool blocks from a chunk of text, leaving only the user‑visible portion. `stripToolBlocks` will replace the block regex with an empty string, then clean up any stray markdown code fences (e.g., empty triple backticks) and collapse multiple blank lines to a maximum of two. Finally, trim whitespace.

When streaming output to the terminal, I want to avoid flashing a partial tool block. The `visiblePrefix` function will locate the first occurrence of the open sentinel; if none is found, it should check for a partial sentinel at the tail of the stream and hold it back, preventing the UI from rendering an incomplete marker. This requires iterating over possible suffix lengths of the sentinel and returning the stream minus that partial piece.

Lastly, when the CLI sends tool results back to the model, I need a consistent formatting. I'll create `formatToolResults` that takes an array of result objects (each with tool name, status, and output) and wraps each in a custom XML‑like tag `<glint:result>` with an index attribute. The whole payload will be prefixed with `[tool results]\n` so the model can easily detect it.

With all that planned, I should now create the file `src/core/protocol.ts` and write the content exactly as designed. This will be the next step in building out the core infrastructure before moving on to the UI layer.

Proceed to write the file with the defined constants, interfaces, regex, and functions.
